teaser.text: AMETEK sells the tools and components that let other businesses measure, control, repair and build things. Its dollar begins with a factory, airline, laboratory or equipment maker and ends, after materials, labor and operating costs, as earnings and cash.

paragraphs.text: It is $219.22 in October 2028, a loss of 11%. It is $225.56 in October 2029, a loss of 7%. The 2029 range is $137.52 to $335.32. Today’s price is $248.17.
Bear has 27%. Base has 53%, while bull has 20%. The table shows how operating results, dividends and valuation combine into those outcomes.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for AMETEK, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base revenue assumptions are $8,600 million in 2027 and $9,000 million in 2028, reaching $9,450 million. Its margins are 20.2% initially and 20.5% thereafter. The bear case uses $8,200 million and $8,300 million, reaching $8,500 million, with margins falling from 18.7% to 18.5%. The bull case uses $8,800 million and $9,500 million, reaching $10,200 million, while margins expand from 20.5% to 21.3%. The bear reflects slower backlog conversion, interest and integration costs; the bull requires rapid synergies and debt reduction. The disclosed $17.8 million of integration costs is treated as non-recurring.

The bear case requires the recent order surge to fade, backlog to convert slowly and Indicor’s financing and integration costs to persist. Earnings weaken, margins stay near 18.5%, buybacks remain limited and investors pay less for each dollar of earnings.

blocks.heading: How much cash does AMETEK really make?

paragraphs.text: AMETEK converts much of its accounting profit into cash, but not all of that cash is available to owners. Operating cash flow reflects collections, payments and non-cash accounting items; free cash flow subtracts spending on equipment and facilities.

blocks.heading: How much does AMETEK pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends are $1.36 per share in the base case for 2027, rising to $1.49 and $1.64. The bear case holds at $1.36, while the bull case reaches $1.40, $1.61 and $1.85. The base tempers the historical 12% annual increases because the acquisition raises financing needs. Still, dividends used only about 17% of 2025 free cash flow, which was $1,671.515 million.

blocks.heading: Is AMETEK’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Across 2021–2025, free cash flow totalled about $7.03 billion. Dividends and buybacks used about $2.16 billion, while acquisitions used about $5.68 billion net of cash acquired. That allocation reveals the central choice: AMETEK returned meaningful cash to owners, but treated acquisitions as the larger engine of growth.

blocks.heading: What is AMETEK’s dividend yield against its price?

paragraphs.text: The table brings these measures together, from the share price and market value to cash yield and dividend yield.

Liquidity and return measures need the same careful reading. The current ratio can look healthy because it includes receivables and inventory, while return on equity can be distorted by goodwill and share repurchases. The dividend yield is only a small part of AMETEK’s capital allocation; acquisitions matter more.

blocks.heading: What has AMETEK guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: On August 4, AMETEK expected 2026 sales growth of 10% and raised its adjusted earnings-per-share outlook to $8.20–$8.30. It also guided to Q3 adjusted EPS of $2.08–$2.10. These are targets for the year and quarter, not a promise that results will rise in a straight line.

On August 26, AMETEK completed its all-cash purchase of Indicor Instrumentation for $5.0 billion. It expects Indicor to contribute approximately $350 million of sales in 2026 and to be “modestly accretive” to adjusted earnings. Accretive means the acquired business should increase AMETEK’s earnings per share after its costs. Management did not give a dollar estimate, and it did not replace the earlier EPS range.

blocks.heading: What do AMETEK's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: June 2026 showed stronger underlying demand and cash generation, although reported margin still reflected acquisition effects. Revenue rose 15.0% year over year, including 10.0% organic growth, so more of the increase came from businesses AMETEK already owned.

Orders rose sharply, and backlog increased. Cash from operations and free cash flow also improved, helped by higher earnings and easier working-capital demands. That combination matters because orders promise future work, while cash shows whether current work is being converted into collections.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in AMETEK's next results?

paragraphs.text: AMETEK scheduled its Q3 release and call for November 3, 2026. Management should explain Indicor’s earnings contribution, integration progress, the amount of acquisition financing and whether cash generation is keeping pace with debt service and maturities.
